notes.meaning: The two angels who had visited Abraham arrive in Sodom as evening falls. Lot is sitting in the city gate, a public place where leaders gathered and business was done. When he sees them, he immediately stands up and bows with deep respect to welcome them. Even in a corrupt city, Lot retained the habit of showing kindness to traveling strangers.

Lot invites the visitors to come to his home, wash their feet, and spend the night safely before continuing on their journey. The angels reply that they plan to sleep in the open town square. Lot knew how dangerous the streets of Sodom were at night, while the angels tested his sincerity and gave opportunity to inspect the city.

Lot urges the travelers so strongly that they agree to enter his home. He quickly prepares a feast and bakes unleavened bread so they can eat without delay. The heavenly messengers ate the food, hiding their true identity for a short time longer.

Before anyone can go to sleep, the men of Sodom surround Lot's house. Men of every age, from the youngest to the oldest and from every quarter of town, join the crowd. This sudden mob showed that the whole city was completely given over to wicked behavior.

The mob shouts for Lot to bring his guests outside so they can sexually assault them. They openly declared their shameful desires without any sense of fear or guilt. Their demands revealed the utter cruelty and moral ruin that brought God's judgment upon the city.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern interpreters hold that the primary sin condemned here was violent inhospitality and abuse of foreign travelers rather than homosexual conduct.

notes.meaning: Lot steps outside to speak with the angry crowd, taking care to shut the door behind him. He put himself in danger to shield his guests from the mob. By closing the door, he hoped to keep the attackers from rushing into the house.

Lot pleads with the men, calling them his brothers and begging them not to do such a wicked thing. He used gentle words to try to calm their boiling rage. Appealing to reason, however, has little effect on people blinded by lust.

In sheer desperation, Lot offers his two unmarried daughters to the mob instead, pleading that his guests must be protected under his roof. While he felt a sacred obligation to care for visitors, sacrificing his own children was a terrible and indefensible wrong. We must never commit one sin in an effort to stop another.

The mob tells Lot to get out of the way, mocking him as an outsider who came to live among them and now dares to act like their judge. They threaten to treat him even worse than his guests, pressing hard against him to break down the door. Wicked people often respond with fury when their sins are challenged.

The two visitors reach out through the doorway, pull Lot back inside, and shut the door tight. The angels used their supernatural strength just as the mob was about to tear Lot apart. God stepped in to rescue His servant at the moment of greatest peril.

The angels strike the violent men outside with sudden blindness, confusing their vision. Even with open eyes, they were so disoriented that they wore themselves out trying to find the doorway. Their physical inability to see matched the deep spiritual darkness in their hearts.

The angels ask Lot if he has any other family members in the city, such as sons-in-law, sons, or daughters. They command him to gather everyone who belongs to him and lead them away right then. Out of mercy for Lot, God provided a way for his whole household to be spared.

The angels tell Lot plainly that they have been sent by the Lord to destroy Sodom. The cries against the city's terrible wickedness had risen straight to God, and judgment could no longer be delayed. Angels serve as ministers of God's wrath against sin just as they do as messengers of His mercy.

Lot runs out to warn the young men promised in marriage to his daughters, telling them to flee because the city will be destroyed. His future sons-in-law do not take him seriously, assuming he is only joking. Because Lot had compromised his life among them, his warning carried no spiritual weight.

At the first sign of dawn, the angels urge Lot to move quickly. They tell him to take his wife and the two daughters still in his house so they will not be swept away in the city's punishment. When God announces judgment, delay is always dangerous.

Even with destruction near, Lot hesitates and lingers, tied to his possessions and home. The angels take him, his wife, and his two daughters by the hand and forcibly pull them outside the city walls. They were rescued entirely because the Lord showed great mercy, not because Lot acted wisely.

Once they are safely outside, one of the angels tells them to run for their lives into the mountains. They are commanded not to look back or stop anywhere on the low valley plain. Escaping judgment requires a complete break with our old sinful environment.

Lot pleads with the angel, begging him not to force them to run all the way to the mountains. Even after being dragged out of danger by a miracle, Lot struggled to trust God's directions. Human fear often pushes us to argue with God instead of simply obeying.

Lot thanks the angel for showing such great kindness in preserving his life, but he still insists the mountains are too far. He worries that the catastrophe will overtake him on the road and kill him. His anxiety caused him to doubt that God could keep him safe in the very place He commanded him to go.

Lot points to a nearby town, pleading that it is only a little place and begging to shelter there instead. He reasoned that because it was small, it might not be as guilty as Sodom and could be spared. He preferred a little city of his own choosing over the refuge God had assigned him.

The angel grants Lot's request and agrees not to destroy the small town he pointed out. God treated His weak servant with remarkable tenderness, answering his plea even though it came from fear rather than bold faith. God often shows great patience toward the prayers of His struggling people.

The angel tells Lot to run there quickly because judgment cannot fall until he is safely inside. Because of Lot's plea about its size, the town became known as Zoar, which means 'little.' God held back His fiery justice until His righteous servant was out of harm's way.

The sun had risen over the earth just as Lot arrived safely in Zoar. The bright morning light made the sudden terror of the coming storm even more shocking. God ensured His servant was sheltered before the fire fell.

The Lord rains burning sulfur and fire from the heavens upon Sodom and Gomorrah. This was not a regular storm, but a direct, supernatural outpouring of divine justice from above. The fiery punishment from heaven matched the burning, unnatural lusts of the people below.

The fiery judgment overthrew the cities, the entire plain, all the residents, and everything growing from the soil. The fertile valley was ruined completely, leaving behind a barren wasteland covered by the Dead Sea. This total destruction stands as an everlasting reminder that persistent sin leads to ruin.

While fleeing behind her husband, Lot's wife looks back toward Sodom and is turned into a pillar of salt. Her backward glance revealed an unbelieving heart that still loved the possessions and comforts of the condemned city. Her death serves as a lasting warning never to look back longingly at a world under judgment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars interpret this as her lagging behind, being suffocated by the heat and fumes, and becoming coated in a thick crust of salt and sulfur.

notes.meaning: Early the next morning, Abraham returns to the high place where he had stood interceding before the Lord. He went back to the place of prayer to see what had happened to the cities. When we pray for others, we should watch with expectation to see how God answers.

Abraham looks down toward Sodom, Gomorrah, and the whole valley, seeing thick smoke billowing up like smoke from a furnace. He realized that the cities were destroyed because ten righteous people could not be found among them. He bowed to God's righteous judgment with deep reverence and solemn fear.

When God destroyed the cities of the valley, He remembered Abraham and brought Lot safely out of the disaster. Lot was rescued not because of his own goodness, but because God was faithful to His servant Abraham who had prayed for him. God hears the prayers of His people and often extends mercy to their loved ones.

Lot becomes afraid to stay in Zoar, so he moves up into the mountains with his two daughters and lives in a cave. He had begged to stay in Zoar, but fear drove him back to the mountains God had commanded him to seek in the first place. Relying on our own plans instead of God's word often leads to loneliness and fear.

The older daughter tells her younger sister that their father is growing old and that there are no men around to marry them in the normal way. Living alone in a remote cave, they feared their family line would die out completely. Their panic caused them to overlook God's moral law in an attempt to solve their problem.

The older daughter proposes that they give their father wine until he is drunk so they can sleep with him and have children. Although they wanted to preserve their family line, their plan was an unnatural and wicked sin. Their actions showed that even though they were out of Sodom, the corrupt thinking of Sodom was still inside them.

That night they get their father drunk with wine, and the older daughter sleeps with him while he is unaware. Lot was so overcome by drink that he did not know when she lay down or when she left. Drunkenness stripped away his good judgment and led him into a disgraceful sin he would have hated while sober.

The next morning, the older daughter tells the younger what she did and urges her to do the same thing the following night. She tells her sister to get their father drunk again so she can also conceive a child. One sin easily encourages another when people justify their wrong choices.

They make Lot drunk with wine again the second night, and the younger daughter sleeps with him while he remains unconscious of what happened. Lot failed to stay on guard and was trapped by the exact same sin a second time. When people let down their spiritual defenses, they easily fall into repetitive traps.

Both of Lot's daughters become pregnant by their own father through this plot. What was carried out secretly in a dark cave soon became impossible to hide. The man who stood firm against the wickedness of Sodom fell into deep dishonor while living in the mountains.

The older daughter gives birth to a son and names him Moab, which sounds like 'from the father.' He became the ancestor of the Moabite nation, which lived next to Israel for centuries. The name she gave him showed a lack of shame, publicly advertising how the child was conceived.

The younger daughter also gives birth to a son and names him Ben-ammi, meaning 'son of my people.' He became the father of the Ammonites, another nation that often fought against Israel. Scripture falls silent about Lot after this point, showing the tragic and sorrowful end of a life shaped by worldly compromise.
